strategies.summary: Implement a custom CUDA prefix-sum fast path for contiguous tensors when the scan dimension is the last axis, flattening outer dimensions into independent rows and assigning one block/warp per row. Keep the existing PyTorch fallback for unsupported layouts or dims.

Use a row-wise scan design: each block handles one or more rows, performing an inclusive scan across the target axis while preserving the original output shape.
For short rows, prefer warp-level scan; for medium rows, use shared-memory block scan; for long rows, process in tiles with carry propagation between tiles.
In forward anchors, dispatch to the extension only for the specialized case and retain torch.cumsum as a correctness fallback.
strategies.expected_gain: High for contiguous last-dimension scans, especially when many independent rows are present and axis length is moderate.

Fallback is still required for non-contiguous tensors and non-last-dimension scans.

review_notes.claude-compatible: Solid, well-scoped fast path for the most common case (contiguous last-dim scan). Row-per-block design is standard and correct. Fallback to torch.cumsum reduces correctness risk. Main limitation: only covers last-dim contiguous case, leaving other layouts unoptimized. Implementation hints are actionable and realistic.

strategies.summary: Use a hierarchical scan strategy inside the CUDA kernel: warp-level inclusive scans for local segments, followed by block-level prefix propagation through shared memory. This aligns with the reduction/scan profile while remaining efficient for varied axis lengths.
implementation_hints: Build the kernel around warp-synchronous primitives first, then stitch warp totals together via shared memory for full-block scans.
Use tile carries so each block can process multiple contiguous chunks of a long row without serializing the whole row on one thread.
Keep launch configuration and wrapper signatures simple in cuda_cpp, while putting tuning constants local to cuda_cu.
Use helpers only to preserve clean extension loading and avoid changing ModelNew I/O.
strategies.expected_gain: Moderate-to-high by reducing synchronization and shared-memory pressure relative to naive per-element accumulation.
risk_notes: Scan is more order-sensitive than reductions, so carry propagation bugs will silently corrupt outputs.
Tuning block size too aggressively may hurt occupancy or shared-memory usage.
Need boundary handling for non-divisible tile sizes.

Moderate value as a design direction but lower actionability.

strategies.intent: Warp-shuffle based prefix scan with vectorized float4 loads
strategies.summary: Use CUDA warp-level primitives (__shfl_up_sync) to perform a prefix scan within each warp without shared memory, then combine warp results via shared memory for the inter-warp prefix. Additionally load/store data as float4 vectors to maximize memory bandwidth utilization.
implementation_hints: Each warp of 32 threads handles 32 consecutive elements of the scan dimension using __shfl_up_sync(0xFFFFFFFF, val, offset) in a log2(32)=5 step loop.
Store warp-level totals in shared memory; a single warp then scans those totals; broadcast carry-back to each warp.
Use float4 vectorized loads (reinterpret_cast<float4*>) when scan_length is divisible by 4 and tensor is 16-byte aligned.
One block per independent row; grid = (num_rows,); block = min(next_pow2(scan_len), 1024).
Expose as cumsum_warp_cuda and dispatch from forward_stmt_2.
strategies.expected_gain: Warp shuffles eliminate shared memory latency for the intra-warp phase; float4 loads double effective memory bandwidth. Expected 2-4x over baseline for medium scan lengths (128-1024).
risk_notes: float4 path requires scan_length % 4 == 0 and proper alignment; must fall back to scalar path otherwise.
__shfl_up_sync requires CUDA compute capability >= 3.0; safe for all modern GPUs.
Warp divergence if scan_length is not a multiple of 32; add boundary masking.

Risks around alignment and non-multiple-of-32 scan lengths are correctly identified. Good risk-adjusted value.

strategies.intent: Hillis-Steele parallel prefix scan kernel for contiguous scan dimension
strategies.summary: Implement a Hillis-Steele (work-inefficient but highly parallel) prefix scan in CUDA. Each block handles one row (the slice orthogonal to the scan dimension). Threads within a block cooperate using shared memory to compute the prefix sum in O(log N) steps. This avoids the sequential dependency of naive cumsum and saturates GPU parallelism for moderate scan lengths.
implementation_hints: Reshape the input tensor so the scan dimension is the innermost (last) axis using permute+contiguous, then restore shape after the kernel.
Launch one CUDA block per row (product of all non-scan dimensions). Block size = next power-of-two >= scan_length, capped at 1024.
Use __shared__ float smem[2][BLOCK] double-buffering; each step reads from one buffer and writes to the other.
After the in-block scan, write results back to global memory. Handle scan lengths not a power of two with boundary guards.
Export the wrapper as cumsum_cuda(torch::Tensor x, int dim) via PYBIND11_MODULE; call _stark_get_extension().cumsum_cuda(x, self.dim) in forward_stmt_2.
Support float32 initially; add AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES for generality.
strategies.expected_gain: 2-5x speedup over torch.cumsum for typical KernelBench shapes (batch x sequence) due to full warp utilization and elimination of cuDNN/CUDA library launch overhead for small tensors.
risk_notes: Hillis-Steele uses 2x more work than sequential; for very long scan dimensions (>4096) a two-pass Blelloch scan may be faster.
Shared memory bank conflicts possible if scan length is a power of two; add padding (+1) to smem rows.
Must handle non-contiguous inputs by forcing contiguous before kernel launch.
Boundary mask required when scan_length is not a power of two.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Reasonable parallel scan baseline, but Hillis-Steele is work-inefficient and the proposal relies on permute+contiguous, which can erase gains. Useful as a simple implementation for moderate sizes, but risk-adjusted value is only moderate.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Hillis-Steele is a proven parallel scan algorithm and the implementation hints are detailed and correct (double-buffering, power-of-two padding, bank conflict mitigation). The 2-5x speedup claim is plausible for moderate scan lengths. Risk: work-inefficiency at large scan lengths is acknowledged but the fallback suggestion to Blelloch is only advisory. Float32-first approach is pragmatic. Overall well-specified.

Initially prioritize common floating-point types and defer uncommon dtypes to PyTorch fallback.
Use the C++ wrapper to centralize argument validation and avoid launching kernels on unsupported layouts.

risk_notes: Overly strict guards may limit coverage and reduce apparent speedup.

strategies.intent: Persistent thread block scan with shared memory tiling for batch parallelism
strategies.summary: For inputs where the batch dimension is large and the scan dimension is small (e.g., batch=128, seq=128), launch a 2D grid where each thread block handles multiple rows simultaneously using shared memory tiling. This amortizes kernel launch overhead and improves occupancy by keeping more warps active per SM.
implementation_hints: Choose tile shape: ROWS_PER_BLOCK (e.g., 8 or 16) x SCAN_LEN threads per block. Grid = (ceil(num_rows / ROWS_PER_BLOCK),).
Each row within the tile is handled by a contiguous group of threads (one warp per row if scan_len <= 32, else multiple warps).
Use shared memory of shape [ROWS_PER_BLOCK][SCAN_LEN+1] to avoid bank conflicts.
Perform Hillis-Steele scan independently per row within shared memory, then write back.
Tune ROWS_PER_BLOCK as a compile-time template parameter; expose multiple instantiations and select based on scan_len at runtime.

risk_notes: Shared memory capacity limits ROWS_PER_BLOCK * SCAN_LEN; for scan_len=128 and float32, 16 rows = 8KB which fits in 48KB shared memory.

Must handle num_rows not divisible by ROWS_PER_BLOCK with boundary guards.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Potentially helpful for batch-heavy small-scan workloads, but more niche and template-heavy than necessary for an initial optimization pass. Decent specialized tactic, though less robust than hierarchical row-wise scan approaches.
review_notes.claude-compatible: 2D tiling for batch-heavy small-scan workloads is a legitimate optimization for specific shapes (e.g., batch=128, scan=128). Shared memory layout and ROWS_PER_BLOCK tuning are well-described. However, the applicability is narrow and the compile-time template instantiation adds complexity. Useful if the benchmark shapes match this profile, but lower generality than strategies 01/02/06.

strategies.intent: Blelloch (work-efficient) two-phase scan for large scan dimensions
strategies.summary: Implement the Blelloch up-sweep / down-sweep exclusive scan (converted to inclusive by shifting) in CUDA. This is O(N) work and O(log N) depth, making it superior to Hillis-Steele for scan lengths exceeding the warp size significantly. Use shared memory for the in-block phase and a secondary kernel for the inter-block carry propagation when scan_length > block_size.
implementation_hints: Phase 1 (local scan): each block computes an inclusive prefix sum over its tile and stores the block-total in a carries array.
Phase 2 (carry scan): recursively or iteratively scan the carries array (small, can use a single block).
Phase 3 (add carries): each block adds its carry offset to its tile.
Use __syncthreads() between up-sweep and down-sweep phases; avoid shared memory bank conflicts with stride-1 access patterns and +1 padding.
Dispatch on dtype with AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES_AND_HALF.
Permute scan dimension to last axis before launch; restore after.
strategies.expected_gain: For scan lengths > 2048, 3-8x speedup over torch.cumsum due to better arithmetic intensity and avoidance of library overhead.
risk_notes: Three-kernel launch overhead may hurt for small tensors; add a fast-path that falls back to Hillis-Steele for scan_length <= 512.
Inter-block carry propagation requires careful synchronization; use cudaDeviceSynchronize or stream ordering between phases.
Exclusive-to-inclusive conversion (shift by one and add first element) must be done correctly.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Technically strong for very long scan dimensions, but likely over-engineered for a KernelBench L1 cumsum task unless shapes are very large. Multi-phase complexity, carry handling, and launch overhead reduce risk-adjusted value.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Blelloch scan is theoretically superior for large scan lengths but the three-phase kernel launch overhead and inter-block carry synchronization complexity are significant implementation risks. The suggestion to fall back to Hillis-Steele for short scans adds complexity. For typical KernelBench shapes this may not outperform strategy_02 in practice. Correctness risk from exclusive-to-inclusive conversion is non-trivial.

Prefer a logical reshape/flatten plan that treats all dimensions except the scan axis as batch dimensions; only use this path when indexing overhead remains reasonable.
If a transpose-to-last-dim approach is used, ensure the output is restored to original layout semantics before returning.
Gate this path behind shape/layout checks so the specialized contiguous-lastdim path remains the primary fast path.
strategies.expected_gain: Moderate by extending custom-kernel benefits beyond the easiest layout cases, improving benchmark robustness across dim choices.
risk_notes: Strided indexing can erase gains if memory access becomes uncoalesced.
Transpose-based handling may add enough overhead to negate benefit on small tensors.
Must preserve dimension semantics exactly, including negative dim normalization.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Useful for coverage, but not the first optimization to pursue. Non-last-dimension support via transpose or strided access adds overhead and complexity, and may dilute gains relative to focusing on the hottest contiguous-lastdim case.
